introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Physics 2 (0780), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2025. Time allowed: three hours.**

Answer ALL questions. Section I is designed to be answered in 1 hour, Section II in 30 minutes and Section III in 1 hour. You are advised to divide your time accordingly. You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers. In calculations you must show all the steps in your working, giving your answer at each stage. Calculators and formulae booklets are allowed.

**Structure of the paper.** SECTION I (One Hour): questions 1 to 5 are compulsory; in question 6 answer EITHER 6 (a), (b) and (c) OR 6 (d), (e) and (f). SECTION II (30 minutes): DATA ANALYSIS, question 7. SECTION III (1 hour): OPTIONS - answer any two questions from the four options (Option 1: Energy resources and environmental physics, question 8; Option 2: Communication, question 9; Option 3: Electronics, question 10; Option 4: Medical physics, question 11).

No data sheet is printed in the paper: whenever a constant is needed, the model answer states the value it uses.
enonce_intro_markdown: $75\ \mathrm{g}$ of steam at $100\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ are passed into a quantity of pure melting ice in an insulated calorimeter. If the heat given out by the steam in condensing to water at $100\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ is just sufficient to melt the ice, calculate the;
incertitudes: Question 2 : aucune constante n'est imprimée. Retenus : chaleur latente de vaporisation de l'eau $L_v = 2.26 \times 10^6$ J/kg et chaleur latente de fusion de la glace $L_f = 3.34 \times 10^5$ J/kg ; avec $L_f = 3.36 \times 10^5$ J/kg on obtient 504 g et la même température, 12.9 °C.

Question 2(b) : « just sufficient to melt the ice » est lu comme : la glace devient de l'eau à 0 °C (sans être réchauffée) et l'eau de condensation reste à 100 °C avant le mélange ; la température d'équilibre est donc celle du mélange de 75 g d'eau à 100 °C et de l'eau de fusion à 0 °C (12.9 °C), et non 0 °C. Seul le total « (4 marks) » est imprimé, sans répartition entre (a) et (b).

questions.corrige_markdown:
Take the specific latent heat of vaporisation of steam $L_v = 2.26\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}}$ and the specific latent heat of fusion of ice $L_f = 3.34\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}}$ (values not given in the paper).

Heat given out by $m_s = 0.075\ \mathrm{kg}$ of steam condensing to water at $100\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$:
$$Q = m_sL_v = 0.075\times2.26\times10^{6} = 1.695\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{J}.$$

This is just enough to melt the ice (at $0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, giving water at $0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$):
$$m_iL_f = m_sL_v \;\Rightarrow\; m_i = \frac{1.695\times10^{5}}{3.34\times10^{5}} = 0.5075\ \mathrm{kg}.$$

**Mass of the ice $\approx 0.51\ \mathrm{kg}$ ($\approx 507\ \mathrm{g}$).**

questions.enonce_markdown: equilibrium temperature of the mixture in the calorimeter.
questions.corrige_markdown:
After the ice has just melted, the calorimeter contains $0.5075\ \mathrm{kg}$ of water at $0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ (from the ice) and $0.075\ \mathrm{kg}$ of water at $100\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ (the condensed steam). The calorimeter is insulated, so heat lost by the hot water equals heat gained by the cold water. Let the final temperature be $\theta$ and the specific heat capacity of water be $c$ (it cancels):

$$0.075\,c\,(100-\theta) = 0.5075\,c\,(\theta-0)$$
$$7.5 - 0.075\theta = 0.5075\theta \;\Rightarrow\; \theta = \frac{7.5}{0.5825} = 12.9\,^\circ\mathrm{C}.$$

**Equilibrium temperature $\approx 12.9\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.** (The heat capacity of the calorimeter itself is not given and is neglected.)
